activity.title: Last week, I led a UX Workshop at work ( Google !) on how to ship your side projects as a designer, with 400+ viewers — with how fast AI is evolving, it's now easier than ever to build and create. But many designers are still super intimidated by the technical side of things or don't know how to get started. I've shipped several consumer side projects to 13k+ users, and have learned a lot along the way — so here's a practical step-by-step guide on how to ship 0-1, modified from my workshop slides! 💡1: Ideation Brainstorming with AI can be pretty awesome. I'm NOT saying to let AI take over your idea; you should definitely use your own creativity. But it can be a fantastic resource for expanding on your thoughts! 🎨 2: Designing I always design first in Figma — but in my opinion, the no. 1 mistake is letting yourself get stuck in the weeds and endlessly iterating because you want your designs to be perfect. Figure out if your goal is shipping or creating a "perfect" product. 🤖 3: Where to build? Vibe coding platforms (Lovable, Replit) are visual first and auto-configure your infrastructure for you, but are not great for complexity. I strongly prefer coding agents (Claude, Codex) for full flexibility and because MCPs instantly solve the problem of configuring/setting up infrastructure etc. 🧑‍💻 4: Setting up You can send a prompt like: "I'm not very technical but I want to build ABC. Help me figure out my tech stack, feasibility of each feature, and how to set up the necessary infrastructure." Ask your agent to connect MCPs to automate the setup! Remember, you can ask for step-by-step instructions for literally anything at any point in time. 🔨 5: Building! Ask your agent to create a plan with multiple stages of development (e.g. MVP features, then auth, then nice-to-have features). For each stage, have a self-contained prompt that can be pasted into a new session to kick off development. Makes this super easy! 🪲 6: Testing & bug-bashing 1. "Spin up multiple subagents to do a comprehensive audit of each part of the codebase." 2. "Use Playwright to walk through my user flows and ensure the flows operate as intended." 3. "Imagine you're XYZ. Simulate using the app and give me a report." 🚀 7: Time to deploy Again, you can just ask your agent for step-by-step instructions. Popular options are Vercel and Cloudflare. With MCPs, you can get your project off localhost in 1 minute — you will need to do this to share your projects with other people. 🦔 8: Adding analytics! I think analytics are so helpful and teach you so much about how to optimize and improve. I absolutely love PostHog — you can watch session replays of users interacting with your UI, create custom insights (not just vanity metrics like MAU), etc. 🌐 9: GTM Figure out where your target users are. Post on social media, do cold outreach etc. More than ever, it's also really important that you show up in LLM summaries. Ask your agent to optimize this (+ do regular SEO) for you. ...more

Megan Yap ’s portfolio reminded me how much room there still is for personality on the web. And honestly, I wish more designers leaned into that. There’s a little mascot wandering around the screen that you can drag around. A visitor card interaction where you leave your own signature. Tiny playful moments everywhere that reward curiosity and make the whole thing feel deeply personal. None of it feels gimmicky though. That’s the important part. Because underneath all the experimentation, the fundamentals are extremely strong. The storytelling is clear, the interaction design is thoughtful, the projects are real, and the craft level holds everything together. That’s why this works. Will this land well with a hiring manager in a large enterprise org? Nah. But it doesn’t want to. Portfolios need positioning and should be opinionated. This is how you can craft something memorable. In Megan's case I even have a visitor card to show for it! My full Portfolio Showcase in the comments ↓ ...more ...more

I spend WAY too much time reading on my phone -- easily 10+ hours some days, usually squinting at size-10 text in the dark. At some point, I realized I’d rather be listening to stories instead. But most audio tools make dialogue sound completely robotic. So I built Tambr (pronounced “timbre” lol). Tambr turns any text into a multi-voice audiobook. Paste, upload, or link anything, and each character gets a distinct voice, with age, gender, region inferred from the story so your characters actually feel real. Just launched today on Product Hunt + I’d really appreciate your support: • Upvote on Product Hunt: tinyurl.com/tambrproduct • Download and leave a review on the App Store: https://lnkd.in/es9WiX5R Shoutout to Sennet S. , Nikhil S. , and Abigail So for all the late-night building sessions 🪻🪻 ...more ...more

After 5 months and countless late night lock-in sessions, Simon Ilincev and I have finally launched Lingofable on the App Store!! Language learning textbooks are often super dull, and memorizing vocab through flashcards means you don't know how to use it in an actual sentence. On the other hand, Lingofable is all about learning naturally through curated stories from fantasy and romance to Reddit-style r/AmITheJerk posts 👀 We utilize research-backed methods to ensure that your library is at a perfect i+1 level, which has been proven to be the most effective for language acquisition! In other words, this is literally the fastest and most enjoyable way for you to improve. If you're learning a language, we'd love for you to try it out! Link is in the first comment :) ...more

It's been heads-down this semester, and super excited to announce that five months, 100k+ lines of code, and a successful beta later, Megan Yap and I have launched Lingofable to the App Store! Lingofable teaches languages through easy, engaging stories from fantasy to Reddit-style threads. It's backed by decades of language-acquisition research on "comprehensible input" and supported by Cornell faculty. Live on the App Store 👉: https://lnkd.in/eEpBGR55 Landing page with info and language-specific waitlists @ lingofable.com . We've been learning languages the wrong way. I've heard so many of my friends say that they have a language learning streak of 300+ but still can't string together a single sentence. They feel like they've been learning for years, but when they try to follow a real-world conversation (let alone participate!) or watch a TV show without subtitles, they still feel like they're lost. Because of this, a lot of people think that they're just not cut out for language learning, but that's not true at all. The problem is actually that most apps and textbooks drill you solely on isolated sentences like "the boy eats the apple", which not only lack context, but are also kinda boring 😭 So as linguistics students at Cornell, Simon Ilincev and I decided to build Lingofable: an app that helps you learn languages through immersion in stories exactly at your level. 1️⃣ Read what you're actually interested in, from fantasy & sci-fi to r/AmITheJerk-style Reddit threads 👀 ngl reading drama is the best way to remember past-tense verbs 2️⃣ The stories automatically adapt to your proficiency, backed by Stephen Krashen's i+1 principle for comprehensible input 3️⃣ Tap to get instant definitions and translations without breaking your flow 4️⃣ Save new words to your favorite SRS platforms (like Anki) to review later I’m currently using it to get my Spanish ready for a trip to Costa Rica! Honestly, it's been so much more fun learning through Lingofable rather than fruitlessly trying to find interesting content online that’s not too easy but also not too hard. We're officially opening the waitlist today! Come and join us as an early tester 🫡 👇 Link to the waitlist is in the first comment! #Lingofable #LanguageLearning ...more

This summer, I had the opportunity to attend the XX International Summer Space School in Samara, Russia! Here at Samara State Aerospace University , I led an international, cross-disciplinary team of students, researchers, and PhD-level scientists in designing a SamSat-LED 3U CubeSat mission. Our team focused on designing an LED-based optical backup communication payload using Manchester encoding. I worked through the full engineering pipeline, supervising and contributing to the link budget analysis, power budgeting, solar panel sizing, and apparent magnitude calculations to assess optical downlink feasibility. Furthermore, we built an FSM-based health monitoring architecture integrating battery, temperature, and solar subsystems. The program wrapped up with a technical defense of our design, which was a great test of how well we understood and designed our own system! Beyond the payload work, this program not only gave me a broader exposure to satellite engineering (mission design, subsystems, attitude control, and small-sat operations) but also the chance to lead and learn alongside an incredible group of researchers, scientists, and engineers from around the world! Reminding us that international and multidisciplinary collaboration is fundamental for the future of space exploration. Thanks, Ohana Berger and Angelo Espinoza , for your endless support in this experience! I am so grateful for this opportunity and for the chance to grow as an engineer and a leader. I can’t wait to carry these lessons into my next chapter. Fun little fact... the last photo in this post has an old Soviet propaganda poster that says "NO! Save it for the nanosatellite!", and honestly, it's the most accurate summary of our power budget discussions jeje...
